chapters.title: Ahaziah seeks Baal-zebub and hears judgment

parts.text: After being injured in a fall, Ahaziah sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub of Ekron whether he will recover. An angel directs Elijah to intercept them and ask whether Israel has no God, since the king seeks a foreign deity. Elijah declares that Ahaziah will die. When the messengers describe him, the king recognizes Elijah.

Ahaziah sends a captain with fifty men to summon Elijah. Fire from heaven consumes that company and a second one. The third captain approaches humbly and pleads for their lives. God tells Elijah to go with him. Elijah repeats the judgment directly to Ahaziah, who dies according to the LORD’s word. Because he has no son, Jehoram succeeds him.

chapters.title: Elijah is taken up and Elisha succeeds him

parts.text: Elisha refuses to leave Elijah as they travel from Gilgal through Beth-el and Jericho to Jordan. Elijah strikes the river with his mantle, and they cross on dry ground. Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit. Chariots and horses of fire separate them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha sees it, mourns, takes the fallen mantle, and parts Jordan on his return.

The prophets recognize that Elijah’s spirit rests on Elisha. They insist on a search for Elijah, but find nothing. At Jericho, Elisha casts salt into the water and announces its healing by the LORD. Later, little children mock him near Beth-el; he curses them in the LORD’s name, and two bears come out and maul forty-two of them.

chapters.title: Water and victory in the campaign against Moab

parts.text: Jehoram of Israel removes a Baal image but continues Jeroboam’s sins. When Moab rebels, he enlists Jehoshaphat of Judah and Edom’s king. Their army runs out of water in the wilderness, and they consult Elisha. Because of Jehoshaphat, Elisha hears their request. The LORD promises water without wind or rain and victory over Moab, instructing them to make the valley full of ditches.

Water fills the country. Seeing it red in the morning light, the Moabites mistake it for blood and assume the allies have killed one another. They rush for spoil and are defeated. Israel devastates Moab’s land and towns. The Moabite king, unable to break through, offers his firstborn son on the wall. Great indignation follows against Israel, and the allies withdraw.

chapters.title: Elisha brings provision and restores life

parts.text: A prophet’s widow faces losing her sons to a creditor. Elisha tells her to borrow empty vessels and pour her small supply of oil into them. The oil multiplies until the vessels are full, allowing her to pay the debt and live on the remainder. In Shunem, a generous woman prepares a room for Elisha. He promises her a son, though her husband is old, and the child is born.

The boy later dies, and his mother seeks Elisha. He returns, prays, and restores the child to life. At Gilgal, he removes harm from a pot of food containing poisonous gourds. Another gift of twenty barley loaves feeds a hundred men with some left over, according to the LORD’s word.

chapters.title: Naaman is cleansed and Gehazi’s greed exposed

parts.text: A captive Israelite girl tells Naaman’s wife that the prophet in Samaria could cure his leprosy. Naaman comes with gifts, and Elisha directs him to wash seven times in Jordan. Angry at the simple instruction, he nearly leaves, but his servants persuade him. He obeys and is cleansed. Naaman confesses that there is no God except in Israel. Elisha refuses payment, and Naaman expresses his intention to worship the LORD alone.

Gehazi secretly follows Naaman and obtains silver and garments through a false story about visitors. He hides them and lies to Elisha. The prophet exposes the deception and declares that Naaman’s leprosy will cling to Gehazi and his descendants. Gehazi leaves leprous as snow.

chapters.title: God protects Elisha and Samaria suffers siege

parts.text: Elisha makes a borrowed axe head float after it falls into Jordan. He also repeatedly warns Israel’s king of Syrian ambushes. Syria sends an army to capture him at Dothan, but God opens his servant’s eyes to surrounding horses and chariots of fire. At Elisha’s prayer the attackers are blinded, and he leads them to Samaria. After their sight returns, he forbids their slaughter and arranges a feast before sending them home.

Later Ben-hadad besieges Samaria, bringing extreme famine. A woman’s account of cannibalism exposes the city’s desperation. The king tears his clothes but vows to kill Elisha. At the prophet’s house, Elisha anticipates the king’s messenger, while the closing challenge questions why they should wait any longer for the LORD.

chapters.title: Samaria’s famine ends as Elisha foretold

parts.text: Elisha declares that food will be plentiful and cheap the next day. A royal officer scoffs, and Elisha says he will see it but not eat it. Four lepers approach the Syrian camp and find it deserted. The LORD has caused the Syrians to hear a great army and flee, abandoning provisions and equipment. After initially hiding spoil, the lepers recognize their duty to report the good news.

The king suspects an ambush, but scouts follow the abandoned trail and confirm the flight. The people rush out and plunder the camp, bringing food prices down exactly as Elisha predicted. The sceptical officer, stationed at the gate to control the crowd, is trampled to death. He sees the deliverance but does not share its food, fulfilling the prophet’s warning.

chapters.title: Restoration for the Shunammite and Hazael’s rise

parts.text: The Shunammite woman returns after seven years away during a famine Elisha foretold. As she appeals to the king, Gehazi is recounting her son’s restoration, and her property and income are returned. In Damascus, Hazael asks Elisha about Ben-hadad’s illness. Elisha foresees the king’s death and weeps over the atrocities Hazael will commit against Israel. Hazael returns, suffocates Ben-hadad, and becomes king.

Jehoram of Judah follows Ahab’s house, having married into it, though the LORD preserves David’s line. Edom and Libnah revolt during his reign. His son Ahaziah also follows Ahab’s evil ways. He joins Joram of Israel against Syria at Ramoth-gilead and later visits the wounded king in Jezreel.

chapters.title: Jehu is anointed and Ahab’s house is struck

parts.text: Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu privately as king over Israel. He announces that Jehu must destroy Ahab’s house and avenge the blood shed by Jezebel. Jehu’s officers learn the message, spread their garments, and proclaim him king. He immediately travels toward Jezreel, where Joram is recovering and Ahaziah of Judah is visiting.

Joram meets Jehu near Naboth’s field and is killed after Jehu denounces Jezebel’s idolatries. His body is thrown into the field in fulfilment of judgment over Naboth’s blood. Ahaziah is also pursued and mortally struck. At Jezreel, Jehu orders Jezebel thrown from a window. Dogs consume her body before burial can be arranged, fulfilling the LORD’s word through Elijah.

chapters.title: Jehu destroys Ahab’s house and Baal worship

parts.text: Jehu challenges Samaria’s guardians of Ahab’s seventy sons, then orders their execution when they submit. Their heads are sent to Jezreel, and Jehu declares the fulfilment of the LORD’s word against Ahab. He destroys the remaining royal associates, kills relatives of Ahaziah whom he meets, and joins Jehonadab in entering Samaria, where the rest of Ahab’s house is eliminated.

Pretending great devotion to Baal, Jehu gathers its worshippers, excludes the LORD’s servants, and has the assembly killed. Baal’s temple and images are destroyed. Yet Jehu continues Jeroboam’s calf worship and fails to walk wholeheartedly in God’s law. God grants his descendants four generations on the throne, while Hazael begins taking Israelite territory. Jehu dies, and Jehoahaz succeeds him.

chapters.title: Joash is preserved and Athaliah overthrown

parts.text: After Ahaziah’s death, Athaliah destroys the royal heirs, but Jehosheba rescues the infant Joash and hides him with his nurse in the LORD’s house. Athaliah rules six years. In the seventh, Jehoiada the priest arranges guards, brings out the king’s son, gives him the crown and testimony, and anoints him before the rejoicing people.

Athaliah hears the celebration and cries treason. Jehoiada orders her taken outside the temple, where she is killed. He establishes a covenant committing king and people to the LORD and binding them to one another. The people destroy Baal’s temple and kill its priest. Joash is seated on the royal throne, the city becomes quiet, and the chapter notes that he is seven years old.

chapters.title: Joash repairs the temple

parts.text: Joash does right while instructed by Jehoiada, though high places remain. He orders dedicated money used to repair the LORD’s house, but the work is delayed. A revised arrangement places a collection chest beside the altar, with the king’s scribe and high priest counting receipts. The money is paid directly to honest workers, carpenters, builders, and stonecutters for structural repairs rather than decorative vessels.

When Hazael threatens Jerusalem after capturing Gath, Joash sends sacred and royal treasures to buy his withdrawal. The king’s servants later conspire against him and kill him. He is buried in David’s city, and his son Amaziah succeeds him. The chapter names the conspirators and records the end of a reign marked by temple restoration but also foreign pressure and internal violence.

chapters.title: Israel’s oppression and Elisha’s final promise

parts.text: Jehoahaz rules Israel in Jeroboam’s sinful pattern, and Syria oppresses the nation severely. He seeks the LORD, who hears and provides deliverance, though the people do not abandon their idols. The army is greatly reduced. His son Jehoash succeeds him and also continues the same sins, with the account briefly noting his strength and war with Amaziah of Judah.

As Elisha is dying, Jehoash visits him. Through arrows shot and struck on the ground, Elisha promises victories over Syria but rebukes the king for stopping too soon, limiting them to three. Elisha dies; later a dead man touching his bones revives. God remains gracious because of his covenant with the patriarchs, and Jehoash recovers captured cities from Hazael’s son in three victories.

chapters.title: Amaziah’s defeat and Jeroboam’s restored borders

parts.text: Amaziah rules Judah with some faithfulness and executes his father’s murderers without killing their children, obeying Moses’ law of individual responsibility. After victory over Edom, he challenges Jehoash of Israel despite a warning against pride. Israel defeats Judah, captures Amaziah, breaks Jerusalem’s wall, and takes treasures and hostages. Amaziah later escapes a conspiracy to Lachish but is killed there. His son Azariah becomes king and restores Elath.

Jeroboam son of Jehoash reigns over Israel and continues Jeroboam’s calf worship. Nevertheless, he restores Israel’s borders according to the word given through Jonah, because the LORD sees the people’s bitter affliction and has not decreed their destruction. His further achievements are noted, and his son Zachariah succeeds him.

chapters.title: Judah’s continuity and Israel’s repeated coups

parts.text: Azariah rules Judah rightly in general, but high places remain. The LORD strikes him with leprosy, and his son Jotham governs the household and people. In Israel, Zachariah is murdered by Shallum, completing the promised four generations of Jehu’s dynasty. Shallum lasts one month before Menahem kills him. Menahem violently punishes resistance, including a terrible attack on pregnant women.

Menahem buys Assyria’s support with money extracted from wealthy Israelites. His son Pekahiah is killed by Pekah, who later loses northern territories and inhabitants to Assyrian captivity before Hoshea assassinates him. Jotham succeeds Azariah in Judah and does right, though the high places remain. He builds the temple’s higher gate. During his reign, Syria and Israel begin attacking Judah, and Ahaz succeeds him.

chapters.title: Ahaz imitates foreign worship and submits to Assyria

parts.text: Ahaz rules Judah wickedly, following Israel’s kings and even making his son pass through fire. He sacrifices at high places. When Syria and Israel besiege Jerusalem, he asks Tiglath-pileser of Assyria for rescue and sends temple and palace treasure as tribute. Assyria captures Damascus, carries its people away, and kills Rezin.

Visiting Damascus, Ahaz sends the design of its altar to Urijah the priest, who builds a copy before his return. Ahaz offers upon it and transfers the regular sacrifices to this new altar, moving the brass altar aside. He also alters other temple furnishings and arrangements in connection with Assyria’s king. Ahaz dies and is buried in David’s city; Hezekiah succeeds him.

chapters.title: Samaria falls and the causes of exile are explained

parts.text: Hoshea becomes Assyria’s tributary but later seeks Egyptian help and withholds payment. Assyria besieges and captures Samaria, carrying Israel away. The chapter explains the exile as the result of persistent sin: worship of other gods, imitation of the nations, idols and high places, child sacrifice, and refusal to heed the prophets. Israel rejects the covenant and follows Jeroboam’s practices until the LORD removes them from his sight.

Assyria settles foreigners in Samaria’s cities. After attacks by lions, a priest is returned to teach them the manner of the God of the land. Yet the settlers combine outward fear of the LORD with worship of their own gods. The account contrasts this mixture with the covenant’s demand to fear the LORD alone and records its continuation among their descendants.

chapters.title: Hezekiah trusts God as Assyria threatens Jerusalem

parts.text: Hezekiah does right, removes high places and idols, and destroys the brass serpent because Israel has burned incense to it. He trusts and cleaves to the LORD, who prospers him. The chapter recalls Samaria’s fall for covenant disobedience. Later Sennacherib invades Judah and takes fortified cities. Hezekiah pays a heavy tribute, even stripping gold from the temple doors, but Assyria still sends a force to Jerusalem.

Rab-shakeh publicly challenges Judah’s confidence in Egypt, military strength, and the LORD. He claims divine authorization for the invasion and urges surrender, mocking the idea that Jerusalem’s God can save it when other nations’ gods failed. He speaks in the people’s language despite the officials’ objections. They remain silent as commanded and report his words to Hezekiah in grief.

chapters.title: God delivers Jerusalem from Sennacherib

parts.text: Hezekiah mourns, goes to the temple, and sends officials to Isaiah. The prophet tells him not to fear Assyria’s blasphemous words: God will cause its king to return home and fall there. Sennacherib sends further threats, claiming Judah’s God cannot deliver it. Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD, acknowledges his sole divinity, and asks deliverance so the kingdoms may know him.

Through Isaiah, God rebukes Sennacherib’s pride, declaring that his conquests occurred under divine purpose and that he will be turned back. Jerusalem will be protected for God’s and David’s sake; Assyria will not enter or besiege it as threatened. That night the LORD’s angel strikes 185,000 Assyrians. Sennacherib returns home and is later killed by his sons while worshipping his god.

chapters.title: Hezekiah’s recovery and the Babylonian visitors

parts.text: Hezekiah becomes mortally ill, and Isaiah tells him to prepare for death. He prays and weeps, and God sends Isaiah back with a promise of healing, fifteen additional years, and protection for Jerusalem. A fig plaster is applied to the boil. As a confirming sign, the shadow on Ahaz’s dial moves backward ten degrees.

Babylonian envoys bring letters and a gift after hearing of Hezekiah’s illness. He shows them all his treasures and armoury. Isaiah asks what they saw and foretells that these possessions will be carried to Babylon and some descendants made eunuchs in its palace. Hezekiah accepts the LORD’s word, acknowledging peace and truth in his own days. His waterworks are noted, and Manasseh succeeds him.

chapters.title: Manasseh’s sins bring a sentence upon Judah

parts.text: Manasseh reverses Hezekiah’s reforms, rebuilding high places, raising altars to Baal and the host of heaven, and placing idolatrous worship inside the LORD’s house. He practices divination, consults spirits, and makes his son pass through fire. He leads Judah into worse evil than the nations previously removed. Through prophets, God announces disaster upon Jerusalem, measuring it by the judgment of Samaria and Ahab’s house. Manasseh also fills Jerusalem with innocent blood.

After Manasseh’s death, Amon follows his father’s idolatrous ways and forsakes the LORD. His servants conspire against him and kill him in the palace. The people execute the conspirators and make his son Josiah king. Amon’s short reign ends with burial in the garden associated with his father.

chapters.title: The law is found and Josiah humbles himself

parts.text: Josiah becomes king at eight and walks faithfully in David’s way. In his eighteenth year he orders temple repairs, entrusting funds to the workers. Hilkiah the high priest finds the book of the law in the temple and gives it to Shaphan, who reads it to the king. Josiah tears his clothes and sends officials to inquire of the LORD, recognizing the great wrath due for failure to obey.

The officials consult Huldah the prophetess. She confirms that the announced disaster will come because Judah has forsaken God and burned incense to other gods. But because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself with tears, he will be gathered to his grave without seeing the coming calamity upon the place.

chapters.title: Josiah renews the covenant and purges idolatry

parts.text: Josiah gathers the people, reads the covenant book, and publicly commits to obey it. He removes idolatrous vessels, priests, altars, groves, and other corrupt practices from the temple and land. He defiles places of child sacrifice and destroys the altar at Beth-el, fulfilling the earlier prophecy of the man of God, whose grave he spares. His reforms extend into former Israelite cities.

Josiah commands an exceptional passover according to the book and removes further abominations. His wholehearted turning is praised, yet the LORD’s judgment upon Judah remains because of Manasseh’s provocations. Pharaoh-nechoh kills Josiah at Megiddo. Jehoahaz succeeds him but is removed and taken to Egypt. Pharaoh installs Eliakim, renamed Jehoiakim, who taxes the people for tribute and does evil.

chapters.title: Babylon takes Jerusalem and deports Jehoiachin

parts.text: Jehoiakim serves Nebuchadnezzar three years and then rebels. Bands from surrounding peoples attack Judah according to the LORD’s word, bringing the judgment associated with Manasseh’s sins and innocent blood. Jehoiakim dies, and Jehoiachin succeeds him. Egypt no longer intervenes because Babylon has taken its former territories in the region.

After a short evil reign, Jehoiachin surrenders Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar. Temple and palace treasures are taken, and the king, royal household, officers, warriors, and craftsmen are carried to Babylon, leaving the poorest behind. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Jehoiachin’s uncle Mattaniah, renaming him Zedekiah. He also does evil. The chapter closes with God’s anger driving Judah toward removal and Zedekiah rebelling against Babylon.

chapters.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a captive king receives favour

parts.text: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem until famine overwhelms it and the wall is breached. Zedekiah flees but is captured; his sons are killed before him, his eyes are put out, and he is taken to Babylon. Nebuzar-adan burns the temple, palace, and houses, breaks the walls, and deports the remaining people except poor workers. The temple’s brass pillars, sea, and other treasures are dismantled and carried away.

Leading priests and officials are executed. Gedaliah is appointed over those left in Judah, but Ishmael assassinates him, and the frightened survivors flee to Egypt. Years later, Evil-merodach releases Jehoiachin from prison, treats him kindly, and gives him a place above other captive kings. Jehoiachin receives royal food and a continuing allowance for the rest of his life.
